title: Ecosystem
content_html:
Ecosystem

Memories are not stored as isolated “records” but are embedded in the physical architecture and ongoing dynamics of the system. Behaviors, cognition, and traits evolve because they increase survival/reproductive fitness within ecological contexts. In organisms, neurons encode memory through synaptic change (plasticity). Plants, though without neurons, “remember” stresses through epigenetic markers, structural growth patterns, or physiological priming (e.g., drought hardening). Ecosystems have legacies (seed banks, soil nutrients, animal paths, species interactions) which embed past events in the living and non-living substrate. This “structural memory” guides how ecosystems respond to disturbance and change.

Evolutionary Psychology’s view is that for animals (including humans), behaviors like fear, cooperation, foraging strategies, or mate choice are not random but evolved to fit ecological pressures. Memory (episodic, semantic, procedural) is tuned by evolution to track regularities in the environment; remembering locations of food sources (hippocampal maps), avoiding predators through conditioned fear, or tracking social relationships (grooming, alliances).

The harmony between ‘embedded memory’ and evolutionary psychology is essentially a feedback loop: evolution shapes the architecture of memory systems in animals (hippocampus, amygdala, prefrontal cortex) and these systems embed experiences within neural structure - the biological analogue of ecosystem legacies. At the individual level, animals recall food patches or predators, at the ecosystem level, seed dispersal patterns, predator–prey dynamics, or soil nutrient cycling preserve the “memory” of interactions. Plants “remember” grazing by altering chemical defenses; animals evolve memory to avoid or exploit those defenses. Pollinators evolve to recall flower timing/shape; plants evolve flowers that exploit pollinator memory and preferences.

Just as we might frame mind as ecosystem, an ecosystem itself is a mind-like structure: past experience is embedded in form, and behavior emerges from feedback and evolution. Plants and animals do not hold isolated “files of memory,” but participate in an ongoing relational remembering across generations.

Co-participants

Thinking of plants and animals as co-participants in an ecosystem, we can frame their “working together” as both conscious (in animals with nervous systems) and non-conscious (plants, microbes, and animals acting through evolved behaviors and embedded legacies). Plants do not have consciousness in the human sense, but they exhibit adaptive responses that appear cooperative: flowering timed to pollinator activity, chemical signalling to attract defenders (e.g., volatile compounds summoning predatory insects), or root exudates shaping microbial communities that, in turn, support animal herbivores. Microbes and fungi facilitate mycorrhizal networks that link trees (“wood-wide web”), indirectly coordinating with animals by regulating nutrient availability and habitat quality. nsects such as pollinators act from evolved preferences and simple memory systems, not deliberate planning - yet their behaviors create reciprocal loops that benefit both plant and pollinator.

Animals (with nervous systems, such as birds, mammals, primates) are essentially social animals, who display intentional behaviors that align with ecosystem partners. Birds intentionally spread seeds by caching, bees and corvids solve problems using memory and reasoning that directly benefit plant reproduction. Humans are conscious ecosystem engineers: agriculture is an intentional co-design between plants and people - selecting and propagating species, whilst conservation and restoration involve deliberate efforts to re-establish cooperative plant–animal interactions.

At a system level, emergent cooperation uses feedback loops to create the appearance of “working together”. For example, pollination mutualisms where plants provide nectar, animals gain food, ecosystems maintain biodiversity. Plants adapt regrowth strategies, animals shape vegetation mosaics, both stabilizing landscapes. The predator–prey balance indirectly supports plant diversity (trophic cascades). This cooperation is not centrally directed but emerges from many small interactions, guided by evolution and memory (genetic, ecological, behavioral).

This can all be viewed as ‘harmony without planning’ - ecosystems embody something akin to Buddhist interdependence, which posits no intrinsic separateness of things, only relations. What seems like “working together” is often each species following its own embedded or evolved rules - yet at the system level, these rules interlock, producing resilience and balance.

The ecosystem

When we talk about an ecosystem, it’s tempting to imagine only plants, animals, and humans. But an ecosystem is far more expansive and multi-layered:

  • Plants: primary producers capturing solar energy.
  • Animals: consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) shaping flows of energy and matter.
  • Humans: ecosystem engineers with conscious foresight, but also subject to the same ecological rules.
  • Microorganisms: bacteria, archaea, protists - unseen drivers of nutrient cycling, decomposition, and symbiosis.
  • Fungi: decomposers, mutualists (mycorrhizae), pathogens - central to soil and plant dynamics.
  • Soil: mineral substrate, organic matter, microbial habitat; it itself is an archive of ecological “memory.”
  • Water: rivers, wetlands, oceans; both habitat and transport medium for energy, organisms, and memory traces (sediments).
  • Air: atmosphere as a shared commons of gases, climate regulator, and dispersal medium.
  • Climate & weather: temperature, precipitation, storms - disturbance regimes shaping resilience and succession.
  • Nutrients & geochemistry: nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon - limiting factors for productivity.
  • Energy flows: sunlight input, heat dissipation, trophic energy transfer.

Microbes release nutrients → plants grow → animals feed → decomposition cycles back. Fire, floods, storms, and human land use reset cycles, but ecological memory (seed banks, soil legacies, cultural memory) guides reorganization. Small-scale microbial shifts can cascade into forest dynamics, whilst global climate patterns constrain local choices (panarchy).

Beyond biology, geology & topography shape water flows, soil depth, microclimates. Solar radiation, lunar tides, planetary cycles set rhythms for life. In human systems, traditional practices are part of ecosystem functioning (e.g., fire stewardship by Indigenous peoples). So the “cooperation” of an ecosystem is not only about species, it’s about living and non-living elements co-constituting a whole system: plants “work with” soil microbes and fungi, animals “work with” climate patterns and landscape corridors, humans “work with” (or against) natural feedbacks, but are never outside them. An ecosystem is a web of relations across life, matter, and energy, not a sum of organisms. Cooperation is emergent from this relational whole - consciousness in some actors, but embedded feedbacks in all.

The universe

Many of the principles we’ve been discussing at the scale of mind and ecosystems echo upward into how physicists, cosmologists, and philosophers think about the universe:

  • Embedded Memory (Legacies in Matter and Energy)
  • Evolutionary Selection (Adaptive Structures)
  • Panarchy / Adaptive Cycles
  • Emergent Cooperation
  • Consciousness and Scale

These principles scale upward. They’re not identical at each level, but they rhyme: neurons, ecosystems, galaxies, and the universe all carry memory, evolve, cycle, and reorganize.

The observational participatory universe.

John Wheeler (1983, 1990) proposed that the universe is not a fixed stage observed from outside but a participatory system: “No phenomenon is a real phenomenon until it is an observed phenomenon.” Quantum mechanics suggests measurement affects reality and Wheeler extended this to the cosmos as a whole. His delayed-choice experiment shows that how we observe light (wave vs particle) can retroactively determine its past behavior. In this view, the act of observation doesn’t just record reality - it brings it into being. The universe is unfinished until observers participate - conscious beings arise within the universe, then “close the loop” by observing it.

In ecosystems, past events remain embedded in structure. In Wheeler’s cosmos, observation leaves a trace that is the structure of reality. In ecosystems, adaptive filtering shapes which traits survive. In Wheeler’s frame, observational choices filter which realities crystallize. Observation is not a one-off - it is iterative and cumulative, shaping emergent order at higher scales. Consciousness itself arises from physical matter, but once present, feeds back to shape the cosmos.

This raises the question: Is consciousness fundamental or emergent? In other traditions (Buddhism, panpsychism) consciousness is relational or intrinsic at every scale. Either way, the act of knowing becomes part of what is known. The participatory universe is not just physics - it’s a way of saying that mind, ecosystem, and cosmos are co-created through observation. Memory, meaning, and reality itself emerge in this participatory loop.

The observer

The Observer–System Split: the observer is outside the system, able to measure without changing it, but the act of observation is part of the system’s dynamics. You can’t separate the observer from the observed. From an ecological point of view, a field ecologist changes the habitat by studying it; a photographer alters what is remembered; even measuring CO₂ affects the system’s trajectory.

If Observer = System, what happens? The concept of a detached observer collapses. Instead, there is only participation. “Observation” becomes just one of the system’s feedback processes, so the “observer” is not outside looking in, but one node among many, whose act of perceiving feeds back into the whole, leaving only system and relation.

  • Relational quantum mechanics (Rovelli): properties don’t exist absolutely, but only in relation to other systems. The observer is just another system in relation.
  • Buddhist interdependence: nothing has independent essence - “observer” and “observed” co-arise.
  • Ecological systems theory: no true outside; humans studying ecosystems are themselves nested within planetary cycles.

If the observer is within the system, the word “observation” is misleading; a better term is co-creation or participation. Neurons recalling a memory reshape the network, species interacting reshape ecosystems. Once you drop the outside observer, the universe is no longer a “spectacle” but a self-experiencing system, Wheeler’s “self-excited circuit” is precisely this: there is no vantage point beyond the loop.

The image, the act of viewing, and the viewer’s memory are the same circuit.
